clue.text: Arrogantly stand-offish and rather drippy

blocks.note: first meaning: haughty and superior, looking down on others
second meaning: with a running nose

explanation.surface: An unpleasant person who is both aloof and a bit wet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drippy' reads as feeble, but here it is literal: a nose that runs.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal adjective means both supercilious in manner and, literally, covered in nasal mucus.

clue.text: see 25dn.
The banks reforming? Glory to God!

indicators.note: reforming means reshaping, so the letters before it are put into a new order

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: A cry of relief at the news that the banks are finally being reformed.
explanation.walkthrough: THANKS BE (to God) is an exclamation of gratitude.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are pious exclamations of praise and gratitude addressed to the Almighty.

clue.text: (& 26ac.) Silent in-yer-face style of humour?

blocks.note: surface reading: aggressive, confrontational comedy
setter's reading: literally in the face, as in the slapstick of silent films

explanation.walkthrough: In-yer-face suggests brash modern stand-up, but silent-film comedians literally threw things into each other's faces.
explanation.definitionFit: The custard pie thrown into someone's face is the classic wordless slapstick gag of silent cinema.

clue.text: Brenda's taken up hint to make way for Brian?

indicators.note: in a down clue, taken up means lifted so that it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, whose cipher is ER
a hint or indication

explanation.surface: Private Eye imagines the Queen finally signalling that she will abdicate in favour of her son.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda and Prince Charles Brian; the 's is 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: To step down from office is to make way for a successor, here the heir to the throne.

clue.text: UKIP-like phone box's dodgy electronic component?

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable and out of order, so these letters are muddled

blocks.note: the letters as written
an integrated circuit, abbreviated IC

explanation.surface: A faulty part in a phone box, oddly described as being like UKIP.
explanation.walkthrough: UKIP is the UK Independence Party, an anti-immigration party.
explanation.definitionFit: The party was widely accused of fearing and disliking foreigners, which is what the adjective describes.

clue.text: Peer who liked his drink, eagerly disposed to accommodate Right

indicators.note: disposed means arranged, so these letters are set out in a new order
to accommodate is to take in a guest, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: the letters as written
the usual abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A nobleman who enjoyed a drink was keen to make room for the political Right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liked his drink' suggests a boozer, but the earl is the one the tea blend was named after.
explanation.definitionFit: The second Earl Grey was a British prime minister and nobleman whose name was given to the bergamot-flavoured tea.

clue.text: As regards a big part of Westminster, it's much to freebie-seekers' liking

blocks.note: on a subject, concerning it
the House of Commons, a chamber of Parliament at Westminster

explanation.surface: A jibe at MPs who love perks paid for by others.
explanation.definitionFit: Something provided free of charge by the establishment is exactly what people chasing freebies want.

clue.text: Moon-walking mate of the Führer?

blocks.note: first meaning: extra-vehicular activity, an astronaut's work outside the craft
second meaning: Hitler's companion and eventual wife

explanation.surface: An absurd picture of Hitler's partner strolling on the Moon.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation stands for extra-vehicular activity such as lunar walks, and is also the first name of Hitler's wife.

clue.text: Potential nepotist? Don't crawl

indicators.note: something potential is not yet in its final form, so these letters can still become something else

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: Advice to someone who might favour relatives: stop sucking up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crawl' suggests toadying, which fits a nepotist; here it means moving slowly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an urging to hurry up, the opposite of moving at a snail's pace.

clue.text: Ffion, abandoned, foot out, extremely lusty? I wish!

indicators.note: out means removed, so the named letter is taken away
abandoned suggests wild and unrestrained, so the letters are scrambled
extremely points to the extremes, the first and last letters of the next word

blocks.note: the name as written
F is the abbreviation for foot, removed here
the outside letters of this word

explanation.surface: A fantasy about Ffion Hague, wife of William Hague, behaving wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: Ffion Hague, wife of the former Tory leader, is a Private Eye regular.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase voices a longing that something were so, the same wistful wish as the exclamation.

clue.text: Miley claims power for the land

indicators.note: to claim is to take possession, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: Miley Cyrus, the American pop singer
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: A pop star staking a claim to political power over a country.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mediterranean island is an independent country, a land in its own right.

clue.text: Call Cameron the head of an unprincipled bunch?

definitions.text: the head of an unprincipled bunch?

blocks.note: to call on the telephone
David Cameron, then Conservative leader and prime minister

explanation.surface: A jibe naming the prime minister as boss of a gang of rogues.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the satirical dig at the government.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringleader heads a group of troublemakers or wrongdoers, an unscrupulous gang.

clue.text: Come to the end of 'Trots', Roth's novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are rearranged into a new form

blocks.note: trots as a verb: moves at a jog
the novelist's name as written

explanation.surface: Reaching the last page of a Philip Roth novel called 'Trots'.
explanation.walkthrough: Trots suggests Trotskyists, but it is a plain verb; 'novel' reads as a book but signals rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: To run short of a supply is to come to its end, having used almost all of it.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) At which village Putin will tolerate no minor encampment (you might say)

definitions.text: At which village Putin will tolerate no minor encampment (you might say)

blocks.note: surface reading: a settlement where a small campsite is banned
setter's reading: camp as in gay; Putin's law banned gay 'propaganda' to minors, at the athletes' village of the Sochi games

explanation.walkthrough: The 2014 Sochi games coincided with Russia's law against promoting homosexuality to minors; camp means flamboyantly gay, and the event had an athletes' village.
explanation.definitionFit: The 2014 games for snow and ice sports were held in Sochi, Russia, under Putin, with an athletes' village.

clue.text: Robin's Left and Right extremes?

blocks.note: surface reading: the political extremes of left and right wings
setter's reading: the bird, whose two wings end at their furthest points

explanation.walkthrough: Left and Right suggest politics, but a robin is a small bird with a left and right wing.
explanation.definitionFit: The far ends of a bird's two wings are the outermost points on its left and right sides.

clue.text: Limp old pop group dropping its last member in hurry

indicators.note: dropping the last member means the final letter of the group's name is lost
in places the shortened group inside the other word

blocks.note: to fly is to dash or hurry
the Swedish band of the 1970s

explanation.surface: A tired old band soldiering on without one of its members.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe flesh or muscle that is soft and slack, lacking firmness.

clue.text: Producing a whopper, holding Bob roughly and applying pressure to member

indicators.note: roughly means approximately, so the letters are not in their exact order
holding means gripping something inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a whopper is a big lie
the letters as written

explanation.surface: Someone telling tall tales while manhandling Bob and leaning on an MP.
explanation.walkthrough: The member is a Member of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Lobbyists try to influence legislators, putting pressure on an MP to support their cause.

clue.text: Bent copper's chief taken to the cleaners

indicators.note: the chief letter of a word is its first, the one at the head

blocks.note: the first letter of this word
to rook is to swindle, the same as taking someone to the cleaners

explanation.surface: A corrupt policeman's boss has been fleeced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent copper' reads as a corrupt policeman, but Bent is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Bent and the answer both mean dishonest as well as physically twisted out of shape.

clue.text: Nick endlessly rattled by sex partner having an easy life

indicators.note: endlessly means without an end, so the final letter goes
rattled means shaken up, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the word as written
a sexual partner

explanation.surface: Nick Clegg, shaken by a lover, while his sex partner lives comfortably.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick may suggest Nick Clegg or a prison; it is just letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes living in comfort and prosperity, like cattle grazing in rich pasture.

clue.text: City corruption: hoarding English money centrally

indicators.note: hoarding means storing something away inside, so one piece is held within the other
centrally points to the middle letter of the word before it

blocks.note: vice is depravity or corruption
the abbreviation for English
the middle letter of this five-letter word

explanation.surface: A headline about corrupt officials stashing away English cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Venice is a city in north-east Italy built on a lagoon.

clue.text: Arm-raisers wanting head from Baby Spice maybe?

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
maybe hints the word could be otherwise, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the first letter of this word
the letters as written

explanation.surface: Bodybuilders hoping for attention from Baby Spice of the Spice Girls.
explanation.walkthrough: Baby Spice reads as one name, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The muscles at the front of the upper arm flex the elbow, lifting the forearm.

clue.text: Take action against a scab? Sounds like it, too!

indicators.note: sounds like tells us to go by how the phrase is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: what you might do to a crusty scab on a wound

explanation.surface: Striking workers confronting a strike-breaker.
explanation.walkthrough: A scab is both a strike-breaker and a crust on a wound; one action fits each sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Strikers picket a workplace to stop strike-breakers, called scabs, from going in.

clue.text: Tax only 10% of Stagecoach's rolling stock?

indicators.note: a tenth of a ten-letter word is just its first letter

blocks.note: the word has ten letters, so a tenth of it is one letter
a train of railway carriages

explanation.surface: A plan to tax just a tenth of the transport firm Stagecoach's trains.
explanation.walkthrough: Stagecoach is a British bus and rail company.
explanation.definitionFit: To tax someone is to place a heavy demand on them, putting them under stress.

clue.text: see 15ac.
(& 2dn.) Board members bound for establishment with balls?

definitions.text: Board members bound for establishment with balls?

blocks.note: surface reading: company directors heading for a posh club or society dance
setter's reading: chess pieces, headed for premises whose sign is three hanging golden balls

explanation.walkthrough: Board members are chess pieces, not directors; the pawnbroker's sign is three golden balls.
explanation.definitionFit: A pawnbroker's premises takes goods as security for loans, traditionally marked by three brass balls.

clue.text: see 4dn.
Is a scrubber possibly putting on blubber for a complete change?

blocks.note: a scrubber cleans
to blubber is to cry noisily

explanation.surface: A cleaner gaining weight, hinting at a total overhaul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blubber' reads as fat, but here it is a verb for crying.
explanation.definitionFit: A total removal of the old order, as when every member is replaced, is a thoroughgoing transformation.
